questions.question: How does backpressure work in Reactor, and what strategies do you use when producers outpace consumers?
questions.title: Reactor Backpressure — Strategies and Practical Handling
questions.direct_answer: Backpressure is the mechanism by which a consumer tells the producer how much data it can handle via **`Subscription.request(n)`** in the Reactive Streams spec. Without it, a fast producer floods a slow consumer and blows up memory. Reactor handles the happy path automatically — operators negotiate demand using a **prefetch** of 256 by default — but when producer and consumer rates mismatch structurally, you choose a strategy: **`onBackpressureBuffer(size)`** (buffer up to a bound; error or drop if exceeded), **`onBackpressureDrop`** (discard silently with instrumentation), **`onBackpressureLatest`** (keep only the newest), or **`onBackpressureError`** (fail fast). Pair with concurrency limits on `flatMap(fn, N)`, prefetch tuning, and observability on buffer sizes. For genuinely mismatched rates, push the work off-process to Kafka or SQS.

interviewer_intent.testing: Real understanding of backpressure beyond the buzzword — strategy selection, when in-process backpressure is enough, and when you must push to an async boundary
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Leaving unbounded buffers in production paths; ignoring backpressure until OOM; misconfiguring `flatMap` concurrency
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss Reactive Streams `request()` semantics, Reactor prefetch math, how HTTP/2 flow control interacts with WebClient, and Kafka as a durable backpressure boundary

sections.title: Why Backpressure Exists — and Why You Rarely Have to Write It
sections.content:
In a push-only system — plain callbacks, Java 8 `Stream` listeners, naive event buses — a fast producer can overwhelm a slow consumer. The results are predictable: unbounded buffering that ends in **OOM**, silently dropped events that nobody notices until the dashboard is wrong, or head-of-line blocking that stalls the entire pipeline.

**Reactive Streams** was designed around exactly this problem.
- The key insight is that **demand flows backward**: the consumer calls `subscription.request(n)` to express capacity, and the producer promises never to send more than has been demanded.
- This is a pull-push hybrid — the demand signal travels upstream, the data travels downstream — and it is what distinguishes reactive composition from plain async callbacks.

In practice, **95% of the time you don't write backpressure code**.
- Reactor operators internally request items in batches (the **prefetch**, typically 256), deliver them downstream, and re-request as consumers drain.
- The system self-regulates.
- You only need to think about backpressure when one of the failure modes shows up: an inherently push source (network stream, Kafka consumer, websocket), a genuinely slow downstream (DB inserts, rate-limited API), fan-out that creates more work than a single thread can handle, or a spiky producer that bursts ten times its steady rate.
- The classic failure signature is a service that **works fine in dev but OOMs in production under load** — that is backpressure that was never designed in.

sections.title: Demand Signal Flow Through a Reactor Pipeline
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Prod["Producer (10K events/sec)"] -->|onNext| Op1[Operator]
    Op1 -->|onNext| Op2["Operator (slow)"]
    Op2 -->|onNext| Cons["Consumer (1K/sec)"]
    Cons -.->|request 256| Op2
    Op2 -.->|request 256| Op1
    Op1 -.->|request 256| Prod
    Prod -.->|overflow| Buffer["Strategy: Buffer / Drop / Latest / Error"]
```

sections.title: The Four Reactor Backpressure Strategies
sections.content:
When a source produces faster than downstream requests, you need to decide what happens to the excess. Reactor exposes four strategies, each suited to a different class of workload.

**`onBackpressureBuffer(size)` — bounded buffering**
- Buffers up to `N` items; raises an error or drops when the bound is exceeded
- Use when short bursts are expected and you can pay the memory for the buffer
- Pair with an explicit `BufferOverflowStrategy`: `ERROR`, `DROP_LATEST`, or `DROP_OLDEST`
- Always log the dropped item — silent drops are worse than failures

```java
incomingEvents()
    .onBackpressureBuffer(10_000,
        dropped -> log.warn("overflow: {}", dropped),
        BufferOverflowStrategy.ERROR)
    .flatMap(this::process, 8);
```

**`onBackpressureDrop` — silent discard**
- Drops items when downstream has not requested capacity
- Use when events are inherently sampleable: telemetry, mouse-move events, redundant ticks
- Always pair with a metrics counter so the drop rate is visible

```java
metricsStream
    .onBackpressureDrop(dropped -> metricCounter.increment("dropped"))
    .sample(Duration.ofMillis(100));
```

**`onBackpressureLatest` — keep only the newest**
- Discards older items in favor of the most recent
- Use when only the latest value matters: UI updates, current temperature, last-known position

```java
sensorReadings
    .onBackpressureLatest()
    .flatMap(this::writeToDb);
```

**`onBackpressureError` — fail fast**
- Terminates the sequence with an error on the first overflow
- Use when backpressure violation signals an upstream bug; you want to fail loudly rather than degrade silently

sections.title: Concurrency, Prefetch, and Rate Limiting
sections.content:
Strategies handle excess; **concurrency knobs decide how much work flows at all**. These are usually the right place to tune throughput vs latency.

**`flatMap(fn, N)` — concurrent inner subscriptions**
- The second argument caps how many inner publishers run at once
- If the source produces faster than `N` in-flight can complete, backpressure naturally applies upstream
- This is your primary throughput knob for any I/O-bound pipeline

```java
source.flatMap(item -> slowAsyncCall(item), 16);
```

**Prefetch tuning**
- Most Reactor operators internally request in batches (default prefetch 256)
- Override per operator: `flatMap(fn, 16, 32)` means `concurrency=16`, `prefetch=32`
- Lower prefetch reduces memory but increases per-batch overhead
- Usually leave the default unless memory is tight or you measured a regression

**Rate limiting operators**
- `limitRate(n)` — splits downstream demand into chunks of `n`; useful for forcing smaller batches
- `limitRequest(n)` — caps total items emitted; one-shot bound
- Resilience4j `@RateLimiter` for per-unit-time limits (10 calls/sec) instead of per-item

**WebFlux and HTTP/2 backpressure**
- WebFlux servers (Reactor Netty) propagate backpressure through HTTP/2 and WebSocket frames
- The server pauses reads when the handler can't keep up
- TCP flow control then slows the sender
- Streaming APIs (SSE, WebSocket chat) scale elegantly under load because of this end-to-end flow

sections.title: Architectural Backpressure — When Reactor Alone Isn't Enough
sections.content:
When the rate mismatch is **structural** (consumer is orders of magnitude slower than producer), in-process backpressure only delays the collapse. You need an asynchronous boundary.

**Pattern 1: Kafka or SQS as durable buffer**
- Fast producer writes to a topic; slow consumer reads at a sustainable rate
- Kafka absorbs spikes; consumer reads at its own pace; you monitor lag
- The right answer for spiky producers and consumers that scale horizontally

**Pattern 2: Bounded queue with a worker pool**
- In-process boundary; reject at the source when the queue is full
- Predictable memory; explicit rejection signals

```java
BlockingQueue<Event> queue = new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(10_000);
// producer: queue.offer(event, 1, SECONDS)
// workers: loop { queue.take(); process(); }
```

**Pattern 3: Reactor `Sinks` for in-process event bus**
- Controlled backpressure with explicit emit-failure handling
- Multicast or unicast sinks; configurable buffer

```java
Sinks.Many<Event> sink = Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(10_000);
Flux<Event> events = sink.asFlux();

sink.emitNext(event, Sinks.EmitFailureHandler.FAIL_FAST);
events.subscribe(this::handle);
```

**Pattern 4: Reactor Kafka consumer**
- Returns `Flux<ReceiverRecord>`
- Consumer requests items; the Kafka client pauses partitions when downstream is slow
- Natural backpressure end-to-end without extra wiring

**WebClient backpressure example**

```java
webClient.get().uri("/big-stream").retrieve()
    .bodyToFlux(Event.class)
    .limitRate(100)
    .flatMap(this::process, 10)
    .subscribe();
```

sections.title: Pitfalls, Decision Guide, and Production Hygiene
sections.content:
**Patterns that bite under load:**
- **Silent drops** — `onBackpressureDrop` without instrumentation loses data invisibly; always log or count
- **Unbounded buffers** — `onBackpressureBuffer()` with no size argument is unlimited; under sustained overload it will OOM. Always set a size and overflow strategy
- **Default `flatMap` concurrency** — may be wrong for your I/O profile; tune per pipeline
- **Hot publishers surprise you** — `Flux.interval()`, `Sinks.many()`, broadcast streams don't wait for subscribers; late subscribers miss events unless configured otherwise
- **Fan-out amplifies** — one source event triggering 10 downstream calls means 10× effective rate; model the math, don't assume upstream rate equals downstream rate
- **Kafka consumers can overrun** — `max.poll.records` plus per-record processing time determines effective rate; fetching 500 records that take 10s to process grows lag continuously

**Monitoring signals to wire up:**
- Operator buffer occupancy (expose via Micrometer)
- Sink buffer occupancy
- Kafka consumer lag
- Bounded queue depth
- Dropped event count from `onBackpressureDrop` callbacks
- `onError` events caused by `BufferOverflow`

**Alert thresholds that work in practice:**
- Buffer above 80% capacity
- Kafka lag above 30 seconds
- Drops greater than zero (when not expected)
- Processing latency drift over baseline

**Debugging backpressure:**
- `.log()` shows `request()` calls; you can see what downstream actually requests
- `Hooks.onOperatorDebug()` adds stack-trace context (dev-only — slow)
- Custom `doOnRequest(n -> logRequest(n))` to inspect demand directly

**Testing with `StepVerifier`:**

```java
StepVerifier.create(
        source.onBackpressureBuffer(5),
        StepVerifierOptions.create().initialRequest(0))
    .thenRequest(3)
    .expectNext(e1, e2, e3)
    .thenRequest(2)
    .expectNext(e4, e5)
    .thenCancel()
    .verify();
```

`initialRequest(0)` means no demand until you explicitly request — this reveals the actual backpressure behavior.

**Decision guide:**

| Scenario | Strategy |
|---|---|
| Short bursts, memory OK | `onBackpressureBuffer(N, ERROR)` |
| Telemetry, OK to sample | `onBackpressureDrop` with counter |
| UI updates, only latest | `onBackpressureLatest` |
| Bug signal when upstream misbehaves | `onBackpressureError` |
| Structural rate mismatch | Kafka or SQS boundary |
| Fan-out work | `flatMap(fn, N)` with appropriate `N` |
| External rate-limited API | Resilience4j `@RateLimiter` or `limitRate` |
| Spiky producer | Kafka + consumer group scaling |

**Virtual threads do not eliminate backpressure.** Loom gives you many cheap threads but does not create I/O bandwidth or downstream capacity. Backpressure is still the right pattern for rate mismatch — you just model it with bounded thread pools and work queues instead of operator chains.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Backpressure is consumer-driven** — `Subscription.request(n)` is the Reactive Streams contract; demand flows upstream, data flows downstream
- **Reactor handles 95% automatically** — operators negotiate demand via a prefetch of 256 by default
- **`onBackpressureBuffer(size)`** — bounded buffer with explicit overflow strategy (ERROR, DROP_LATEST, DROP_OLDEST)
- **`onBackpressureDrop`** — for sampleable streams; always pair with a metric counter
- **`onBackpressureLatest`** — UI / current-value scenarios
- **`onBackpressureError`** — fail fast when overflow signals an upstream bug
- **`flatMap(fn, N)`** is the primary concurrency / throughput knob for I/O-bound pipelines
- **Kafka or SQS** is the right answer for structural rate mismatches
- **Never leave unbounded buffers** in production paths

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Backpressure is the mechanism by which a consumer tells the producer how much data it can handle through `Subscription.request(n)` in the Reactive Streams spec. Without it, a fast producer floods a slow consumer and blows up memory.

**How it works under the hood:**
- Demand flows backward: the consumer requests `n`, and the producer promises no more than that
- It's a pull-push hybrid — demand signal upstream, data downstream
- Reactor operators request in batches via prefetch (256 default)
- The system self-regulates 95% of the time

**When backpressure becomes your problem:**
- Inherently push sources — network stream, Kafka, websocket
- Slow downstream — DB inserts, rate-limited API
- Fan-out creating more work than one thread can handle
- Tight memory budget; can't buffer indefinitely
- Spiky producers bursting 10× steady rate

**The four Reactor strategies:**
- **`onBackpressureBuffer(size)`** for short bursts when you can pay the memory; always with overflow strategy
- **`onBackpressureDrop`** for sampleable streams; always with a counter so drops are visible
- **`onBackpressureLatest`** when only the most recent value matters
- **`onBackpressureError`** when a violation signals a bug — fail loudly

**Concurrency control:**
- `flatMap(fn, N)` caps concurrent inner subscriptions; primary throughput knob
- Prefetch override `flatMap(fn, N, prefetch)` for memory-tight pipelines

**When in-process isn't enough:**
- Kafka or SQS as durable async boundary
- Reactor `Sinks` for in-process event bus with controlled backpressure
- Reactor Kafka returns `Flux<ReceiverRecord>` with end-to-end backpressure to the broker

**The strategic answer:** reactive's value is making backpressure explicit.
- Pick a strategy per pipeline and document the trade-off; monitor buffer sizes and drop counts; for structural mismatches, push to Kafka or SQS; never leave unbounded buffering in production.
- Virtual threads don't eliminate backpressure — they just change how you model it.

questions.question: How do you tune flatMap concurrency and prefetch in Reactor for production throughput?
questions.title: flatMap Concurrency and Prefetch — Tuning Reactor Throughput
questions.direct_answer: **`flatMap(fn, concurrency, prefetch)`** is Reactor's main throughput knob. The `concurrency` argument caps how many inner publishers run at once — directly controlling parallel I/O. The `prefetch` argument sets how many items each operator requests from upstream in a batch (default 256). For I/O-bound pipelines (HTTP, R2DBC), tune `concurrency` to match the downstream pool size; for CPU-bound work, use `parallel()` instead. Lower `prefetch` reduces memory at the cost of more upstream `request()` calls. The wrong defaults cause two opposite failures: too low concurrency under-uses capacity, too high concurrency exhausts connection pools or upstream rate limits.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can reason about Reactor's internal demand mechanics and tune them against real-world resource limits (DB pools, HTTP semaphores, rate limits)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating `flatMap` as if it had unbounded concurrency in old Reactor versions, or leaving the default 256 against a 10-connection pool
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss `flatMapSequential` vs `concatMap` ordering, when to switch to `parallel().runOn(scheduler)`, and how prefetch tuning affects memory under bursty loads

sections.title: Why `flatMap` Defaults Sometimes Break Production
sections.content:
**`flatMap`** is the workhorse operator for asynchronous transforms — every time you call a remote service, query a database, or fan out to multiple inner publishers, you go through `flatMap`. By default it allows up to **`Queues.SMALL_BUFFER_SIZE`** (typically 256) concurrent inner subscriptions and uses a prefetch of the same size for upstream demand.

Those defaults are reasonable for a CPU-bound transform but **dangerous for I/O against a small pool**.
- If your service makes downstream HTTP calls and the WebClient connection pool holds 50 connections, a `flatMap` with concurrency 256 will issue requests far faster than the pool can serve.
- Connections queue, latency balloons, and a slow downstream becomes a cascading outage.

The **right concurrency value** is rarely a guess: it should match (or be slightly less than) the downstream capacity — connection pool size, rate limit, or the consumer's true throughput.
- Prefetch is a secondary knob that trades memory for upstream `request()` overhead.
- Tuning these explicitly per pipeline is what separates a service that survives a Black Friday spike from one that doesn't.

sections.title: What Each `flatMap` Argument Actually Does
sections.content:
**Signature:** `flatMap(Function<T, Publisher<R>> fn, int concurrency, int prefetch)`

**`concurrency` — concurrent inner subscriptions**
- Caps the number of inner publishers Reactor subscribes to simultaneously
- When the cap is reached, additional source items wait — naturally generating upstream backpressure
- Match this to the downstream resource limit: HTTP pool size, DB pool size, or external API rate limit

**`prefetch` — upstream batch size**
- Tells the operator how many items to request from upstream in each `request(n)` call
- Default 256; lower values reduce in-flight memory but trigger more `request()` round-trips
- Rarely needs tuning unless the upstream items are large (megabyte payloads) or memory is tight

**The single-arg form** `flatMap(fn)` uses the default `Queues.SMALL_BUFFER_SIZE` for both — fine for in-memory transforms, dangerous for external I/O.

**Worked example:** an HTTP fan-out against a 50-connection pool.

```java
source
    .flatMap(id -> webClient.get().uri("/items/{id}", id)
            .retrieve().bodyToMono(Item.class),
        50)
    .subscribe(this::handle);
```

With `concurrency=50`, the pipeline issues at most 50 in-flight HTTP calls. The 51st `id` waits for one of the in-flight calls to complete, which automatically pauses upstream demand.

sections.title: Choosing `flatMap`, `concatMap`, or `flatMapSequential`
sections.content:
Concurrency is one axis; **ordering is another**. Reactor exposes three flatMap variants for the trade-off.

**`flatMap` — interleaved, fastest**
- No ordering guarantee — inner publishers complete in arbitrary order
- Highest concurrency; best throughput
- Use when downstream consumers don't care about order

**`flatMapSequential` — ordered, still concurrent**
- Inner publishers run concurrently up to the limit, but emissions are buffered and released in source order
- Buffering cost: memory grows when an early item is slow and later items finish first
- Use when ordering matters but you can pay the memory tax

**`concatMap` — strict serial**
- Subscribes to one inner publisher at a time, in order
- Effective concurrency is 1 — slow but predictable
- Use when ordering is critical and downstream cannot tolerate buffering (e.g., writing to a Kafka partition where order must be preserved)

```java
ordersFlux.concatMap(o -> kafkaSender.send(partitionedRecord(o)));
```

**Decision shortcut:**
- Ordering doesn't matter → `flatMap`
- Ordering matters, throughput matters → `flatMapSequential`
- Ordering is sacred, throughput secondary → `concatMap`

sections.title: When to Switch to `parallel()` Instead
sections.content:
`flatMap(fn, N)` is the right tool for **I/O-bound** concurrency — calls that mostly wait. For **CPU-bound** transforms (image processing, JSON parsing of huge payloads, crypto), you want true CPU parallelism on the parallel scheduler.

**`parallel()` + `runOn(Schedulers.parallel())`**

```java
Flux.range(1, 10_000)
    .parallel(Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors())
    .runOn(Schedulers.parallel())
    .map(this::cpuHeavyTransform)
    .sequential()
    .subscribe();
```

**How it differs from `flatMap`:**
- `parallel(n)` splits the flux into `n` rails; each rail runs on a separate thread
- `runOn(scheduler)` is required — without it the rails are no-ops
- `sequential()` merges rails back into a single Flux for downstream operators
- Designed for synchronous CPU work, not async I/O

**Rule of thumb:**
- I/O-bound (HTTP, DB) → `flatMap(fn, concurrency)`
- CPU-bound transform → `parallel(N).runOn(parallel())`
- Blocking call you can't replace → `flatMap(item -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> blocking(item)).subscribeOn(boundedElastic()), N)`

sections.title: Tuning Pitfalls and Production Hygiene
sections.content:
**When the defaults bite:**
- **DB pool exhaustion** — `flatMap` with default 256 against an R2DBC pool of 10 means 246 items wait per cycle for a connection; latency spikes
- **Upstream rate limit hits** — fanning out 256 concurrent calls to an API limited at 100/sec returns 429s
- **Memory under bursty load** — high prefetch buffers items in flight; spiky payload sizes can multiply that into a heap problem
- **Order surprises** — code that worked because items happened to arrive in order breaks under load when concurrency increases

**How to choose `concurrency`:**
- HTTP fan-out → set to `min(pool size, expected downstream concurrency)`
- Database fan-out → set to `min(R2DBC pool size, db CPU / query cost)`
- Rate-limited API → set to `floor(rate_limit_per_second × p99_latency_seconds)` (Little's Law)
- Internal in-memory transforms → leave default; they finish in microseconds

**How to choose `prefetch`:**
- Default (256) is right for most cases
- Lower (32 or 8) when items are large or memory is tight
- Higher rarely helps; the gain over 256 is usually noise

**Diagnostic patterns:**
- Add `.doOnRequest(n -> log.debug("req {}", n))` upstream of `flatMap` to see actual demand
- Watch downstream pool metrics (`reactor.netty.connection.provider.acquire.time`, `r2dbc.pool.pending`) — pool waits indicate `concurrency` is too high
- p99 latency growing while throughput stays flat → downstream saturated; reduce `concurrency`

**Anti-patterns:**
- Setting concurrency to `Integer.MAX_VALUE` to "go fast" — guarantees a downstream outage
- Using `flatMap` for serial workflows where `concatMap` is what you want
- Tuning `prefetch` without measuring — usually no benefit, sometimes regressions

**The 80/20 of tuning:** for most production WebFlux services, the only knob you actually touch is `concurrency` — set it to match the downstream pool. Prefetch defaults are fine.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`flatMap(fn, concurrency, prefetch)`** — concurrency caps in-flight inner publishers; prefetch sets upstream batch size
- **Default concurrency** is `Queues.SMALL_BUFFER_SIZE` (256) — too high for small downstream pools
- **Match concurrency to downstream capacity** — HTTP pool, R2DBC pool, or rate limit
- **`flatMap` is for I/O-bound** work; `parallel().runOn(parallel())` for CPU-bound
- **`concatMap`** for strict ordering at the cost of concurrency
- **`flatMapSequential`** for ordered emissions with concurrent execution and buffering cost
- **Prefetch defaults rarely need changing** — touch only when item size or memory pressure forces it
- **Diagnose with `doOnRequest`** and downstream pool metrics; pool waits mean concurrency is too high

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`flatMap` is Reactor's main concurrency knob, and its defaults — concurrency 256, prefetch 256 — are dangerous for I/O against small pools.

**The two arguments:**
- `concurrency` caps in-flight inner publishers; when full, source items wait, naturally generating backpressure
- `prefetch` is the upstream batch size for `request()` calls; default 256 is fine for most workloads

**Choosing concurrency:**
- HTTP fan-out → match WebClient pool size
- DB fan-out → match R2DBC pool size
- Rate-limited API → `rate_limit × p99_latency` (Little's Law)
- In-memory transforms → leave default

**flatMap vs flatMapSequential vs concatMap:**
- `flatMap` for max throughput, no ordering
- `flatMapSequential` for ordered emissions with concurrent execution and a buffering memory cost
- `concatMap` for strict serial when ordering is sacred

**flatMap vs parallel:**
- `flatMap(fn, N)` for I/O-bound — calls that mostly wait
- `parallel(N).runOn(Schedulers.parallel())` for CPU-bound transforms
- For blocking calls, wrap with `Mono.fromCallable(...).subscribeOn(boundedElastic())` inside a `flatMap`

**Production diagnostic:** if p99 latency grows while throughput stays flat, downstream is saturated — reduce concurrency. If throughput plateaus far below downstream capacity, increase it. The 80/20 of tuning is just matching `flatMap` concurrency to the downstream pool.
